title: Container Fundamentals: Why & How Isolation Works
summary: What a container actually is at the OS level, and why it is not "a lightweight VM."

slides.markdown:
A container is a **process on your existing kernel** that's been made to believe it's alone on the machine — its own filesystem, its own process tree, its own network stack — while a VM is a whole separate computer, kernel included, simulated in software.

That one distinction — sharing the host kernel vs virtualizing an entire machine — explains almost everything about why containers start in milliseconds and VMs take minutes.

slides.subTitle: What's shared vs what's virtualized
slides.markdown:
The architectural difference is the kernel: containers share the host's, VMs each run their own.

![Containers vs VMs: shared kernel vs virtualized hardware](assets/containers-vs-vms.svg)

A VM's hypervisor virtualizes hardware, and each VM boots a full guest OS with its own kernel — heavy, but kernel-isolated. A container has no guest kernel: an isolated process on the host kernel, starting instantly but with a weaker security boundary.

assets.alt: Containers vs VMs: shared kernel vs virtualized hardware

slides.subTitle: The isolation primitive
slides.markdown:
**Namespaces** are the kernel feature that gives a process its own isolated view of a global resource. The ones that matter: **PID** (its own process tree, so PID 1 inside the container isn't PID 1 on the host), **net** (its own network interfaces and routing table), **mount** (its own filesystem view), **UTS** (its own hostname), **IPC** (its own inter-process communication namespace), and **user** (its own UID/GID mapping, so root inside can map to an unprivileged user outside).

A container is, at its core, just a process launched into a fresh set of these namespaces.

slides.subTitle: The resource-limiting primitive
slides.markdown:
**cgroups** (control groups) are the kernel feature that caps and accounts for how much CPU, memory, and I/O a process (or group of processes) can consume. Where namespaces answer "what can you *see*," cgroups answer "how much can you *use*."

When you set a container's memory limit, you're writing a value into a cgroup; when the container exceeds it, the kernel's OOM killer terminates a process inside that cgroup — the host and other containers are untouched.

slides.subTitle: How an image becomes a running filesystem
slides.markdown:
A container image is stored as a stack of read-only **layers**, each representing one change (installing a package, copying a file). A **union filesystem** merges these layers into a single coherent view at runtime, and adds one thin **writable layer** on top for anything the running container changes.

Multiple containers from the same image share the exact same read-only layers on disk — only their writable layers differ — which is why spinning up ten containers from one image costs almost no extra disk space.

slides.subTitle: What "container" means underneath the word
slides.markdown:
A running container is the combination of three kernel features acting on one ordinary process: **namespaces** give it an isolated view of the world, **cgroups** cap what it can consume, and a **union filesystem** gives it a private-looking root filesystem assembled from shared, read-only image layers.

There's no separate "container kernel object" — it's a completely normal Linux process that the kernel has been told to isolate and limit in these specific ways.

slides.subTitle: A syscall-level view of `docker run`
slides.markdown:
Roughly, `docker run` triggers this sequence of kernel-level calls:

```
clone(CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNET | CLONE_NEWNS | ...)  # new namespaces
pivot_root(/var/lib/docker/.../merged)                  # switch to the image's fs
write(cgroup.procs, pid)                                # join the cgroup
execve("/app/start")                                    # run the container's process
```

`clone()` (not `fork()`) is what creates the new namespaces at process-creation time; `pivot_root` swaps the process's view of the filesystem to the union-mounted image; and joining a cgroup applies the resource limits — all before your actual application code ever runs.

**Wrong belief:** "Containers are more secure than VMs by default, since they're isolated."

**Why it's wrong:** because containers share the host kernel, a kernel-level vulnerability can let a process escape its container and reach the host or other containers — a boundary a VM's separate kernel doesn't share. Containers isolate normal operation, not every attack a hypervisor blocks.

**Correct model:** containers give lightweight, fast isolation; VMs give a stronger security boundary. Sensitive multi-tenant workloads often run containers *inside* VMs for both.

slides.subTitle: How a container differs from a VM
slides.markdown:
When asked to differentiate containers from VMs, lead with the kernel: "a container is a process isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups, sharing the host kernel; a VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own full kernel." Then draw the consequence — containers start in milliseconds and pack denser per host; VMs take longer to boot but isolate more strongly.

Closing with "that's why containers often run inside VMs in the cloud — fast packing plus a hypervisor boundary" shows you see them as complementary, not competitors.
